The sensor schedule delivered 30 liters of water across its six trays during the fourteen-day pilot.

Document evidence:
[S1] 1 Motivation (p.1–1)
The Cedar pilot examined greenhouse water use by comparing a timer‑based irrigation schedule with a moisture‑sensor schedule over fourteen days under identical greenhouse conditions. Six trays with the same soil and seedlings were assigned to each schedule; daily irrigation volume was recorded and plant height measured at the study’s end. The goal was to reduce unnecessary irrigation while maintaining growth, not to assess outdoor farms or long‑term yields. The same caretaker inspected both groups each morning, and any equipment failures were logged before daily totals were calculated.

[S2] 2 Timer Results (p.2–2)
The timer schedule delivered 42 L of water across six trays during a fourteen‑day pilot, operating at fixed intervals independent of soil moisture. Daily records noted some irrigation occurred while soil was already moist, but no timer failures were reported. The timer group’s mean final plant height was 18 cm; water volume reflects total irrigation, not per‑tray amounts, and height is a group mean measured at the end. No variance estimates or significance tests were provided. Authors suggest future tests use different soils, larger groups, and longer observation periods.

[S3] 3 Sensor Results (p.3–3)
The sensor schedule delivered 30 L of water across six trays in a fourteen‑day pilot. Mean final plant height was 19 cm. Irrigation was triggered when moisture fell below the configured threshold; one loose cable was repaired before day 1 and no failures occurred. The pilot observed lower total water use with the sensor schedule while achieving a similar final plant height. Authors note the report does not establish causality or long‑term yield, limit findings to the tested trays and conditions, and recommend a larger controlled trial, further threshold calibration, and sensor maintenance study.
